automation_evidence.finding: USDOT-published study: drivers are detained beyond the 2-hour free time on roughly 1 in 10 stops, for an average of 1.4 extra hours (3.4 hours total at the facility); for-hire truckload carriers are detained about 5x as often as private carriers, so appointment/dock coordination is a concrete source of lost driver hours.

Peer-reviewed regression on 16,227 shipment records at a large US shipper: private fleets experience less detention than for-hire carriers, and facility operating hours and cargo-processing speed drive the gap - i.e., facility-side workflow (not driving) is where the time leaks.

Peer-reviewed simulation of an adaptive truck-appointment system at a container port using real-world data: only 7.8% of truck arrivals had to be rescheduled, maximum queue length fell ~62%, and ~785 tons/yr of CO2 were avoided (total 1,281 tons/yr) versus baselines.

Peer-reviewed game-theoretic model of terminal/drayage appointment setting finds lower gate-waiting cost than a single-player optimization, with savings growing as the number of appointments per truck increases - suggests coordination value is shared between terminal and carrier, so a single-party agent captures only part of it.

Preprint evaluating an LLM-augmented freight broker over 115,125 negotiations: keeping pricing in a deterministic formula and using the LLM only as a language layer achieved agreement rates and broker savings comparable to an unconstrained 20-billion-parameter LLM broker, with negligible inference cost and auditable decisions.

Preprint constructing abilities-based robotics/AI exposure indices for 774 occupations and 250 NAICS industries: trucking and warehousing rank among the most exposed industries to physical automation, but the authors state the measure captures technical relatedness, not readiness, cost or adoption.

Preprint showing LLM-generated behavior trees coordinated an excavator and a dump truck with up to 93% success across 30 simulated instruction scenarios and in real-machine tests - early evidence that LLM planning can drive yard/loading equipment, not over-the-road freight.

common_tools: Transportation management systems (TMS) such as McLeod LoadMaster, Trimble/TMW, MercuryGate (named here from general industry knowledge, not a local survey)
Load boards and rate benchmarks: DAT, Truckstop (market rate data feeds quoting and margin decisions)
Telematics / ELD platforms: PeopleNet, Omnitracs, Samsara, Motive, Geotab (O*NET lists PeopleNet and Omnitracs for truck drivers; others are common industry systems)
Routing and mileage: ALK Technologies PC*MILER, MarcoSoft Quo Vadis (both listed in O*NET software skills for 53-3032)
ERP / accounting: SAP, ADP ezLaborManager (O*NET), plus QuickBooks/NetSuite in small carriers (general knowledge)
EDI X12 transactions (204 load tender, 214 shipment status, 990 responder) and email/Outlook as the de facto broker-carrier channel (Outlook listed in O*NET for 43-5011)
Visibility and tracking platforms such as project44 / FourKites (general industry knowledge)
Port/drayage: terminal appointment and container-status systems (eModal-style portals) plus terminal-specific systems at Port Newark/Elizabeth (general knowledge; not verified in a fetched source)
Driver log/paperwork utilities: TruckersHelper, Fog Line Software Truckn Pro, DDL drivers daily log (listed in O*NET software skills for 53-3032)
constraints: FMCSA hours-of-service rules and the electronic logging device mandate mean driver hours must be recorded by a certified, driver-attributed system with a tamper-evident audit trail; an AI agent can read and flag HOS data but cannot author or edit it.

Broker and forwarder obligations: 49 CFR Part 371 requires records of brokerage transactions to be kept and produced on request, so quoting/booking agents need durable, exportable records rather than chat-only logs.

Household goods moving is separately regulated (49 CFR Part 375: written estimates, bills of lading, arbitration/dispute process) - a key constraint for moving & storage members of this industry group.
Hazardous materials shipments require shipping papers and emergency response information (49 CFR Part 172), so document automation must be conservative and human-verified on hazmat lanes.

Drayage and port work involves TWIC-credentialed drivers and terminal-controlled access; appointment and gate data lives in third-party terminal systems, so agents must integrate with external portals rather than own the workflow.

Driver personal data (CDL, medical certificates, drug & alcohol Clearinghouse status, location traces) is sensitive personal information; carrier customers and insurers generally expect it to stay in private/contracted environments, favoring private or on-prem deployments over public consumer LLM endpoints.
Shipper-specific rates, accessorials and contract terms are commercially confidential between broker and customer, which argues for tenant-isolated models and strict data-retention controls.
Legacy integration load: small carriers and brokers run a mix of TMS, spreadsheets, EDI VANs and email; agents must tolerate unstructured PDFs, scans and phone calls rather than clean APIs.
trends: New Jersey is a heavy freight-labor state: 52,580 heavy/tractor-trailer drivers and 108,090 hand freight/stock movers in May 2023, with movers at 1.30x national employment concentration (BLS OEWS NJ).
National driver demand is projected to grow only about as fast as average: 2,221,200 jobs (2025) to 2,305,000 (2035), +4% / +83,800 (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2025-35 projections).

Detention and facility wait time remain a structural productivity leak in truckload operations, with for-hire truckload carriers most exposed (USDOT 2014 study; 2025 peer-reviewed shipper-data study).
Port drayage is steadily moving toward appointment-based gate access, with an active research literature on adaptive and auction-based appointment systems aimed at cutting queues and turn times.

Wage pressure is concentrated in the mid-skill clerical layer (freight agents ~$28.80/hr, dispatchers ~$24.32/hr, shipping clerks ~$20/hr in NJ), which is exactly the layer that status calls, quoting and document prep consume.

Labor-market tightness plus thin brokerage margins push operators toward automating coordination work rather than adding headcount; the strongest measured effects in the literature are on scheduling/queue and negotiation tasks, not on driving.
caveats: Wage figures are BLS OEWS May 2023 estimates for New Jersey as published on the BLS state page (page last modified April 2024), retrieved through the Internet Archive because BLS retired the /oes/current/ state pages during its 2025-2026 site restructuring; newer May 2024/May 2025 state tables could not be retrieved, and the NJ Department of Labor OEWS tables are distributed as .xlsx files that this tool could not parse. The May 2023 file is built from three years of survey panels, so it lags current pay. No Middlesex-County-specific OEWS cut was retrieved: under current OMB delineations Middlesex County sits inside the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area, and NJ DOL's county/Middlesex-Monmouth-Ocean tables were not machine-readable here, so statewide figures are used as the benchmark. O*NET task lists are national occupational descriptions, not observations of NJ firms. Automation evidence is thin and mostly not freight-specific: the detention studies measure the problem rather than an AI fix; the appointment-system papers are simulations or single-port models; the freight-negotiation and robotics-exposure items are arXiv preprints, not peer-reviewed journal articles, despite being labeled 'peer-reviewed' in study_type to match the schema (treat them as Medium/Low). Several peer-reviewed findings were read from indexed abstracts (OpenAlex records) rather than publisher full text, because publisher pages returned 403/paywall. No vendor case studies were used. Tool names marked 'general industry knowledge' were not verified against a fetched source.
data_gaps: No May 2024 or May 2025 New Jersey OEWS wage table could be retrieved (BLS /oes/ state pages redirect to a JavaScript data explorer; the BLS public API rejected requests with a daily-limit error).

No Middlesex County or Edison/New Brunswick metro wage cut: the legacy Edison-New Brunswick MSA no longer exists, and NJ DOL county workbooks (.xlsx) were not parseable by the available fetch tooling.
No NJ-specific measurement of time saved or error reduction from AI agents at carriers, brokers or movers was found; the closest evidence is national detention research and non-US port simulations.

No accessible source for ATA/ATRI driver-shortage estimates or ATRI operating-cost benchmarks (fmcsa.dot.gov and truckingresearch.org returned 403/JS-only pages; web search was unavailable during this run).

Independent measurement of document-AI accuracy on bills of lading, rate confirmations or PODs (precision/recall or hours saved) was not located; the freight-forwarding automation papers surfaced were low-quality/unreviewed and were excluded.

Port of New York and New Jersey truck turn-time and appointment data (PANYNJ Council on Port Performance) was not retrieved - panynj.gov paths tried returned 404, and no search engine was available to locate the current URL.

Web search providers (Exa, OpenAI) were rate-limited or over quota for the entire run, so coverage depends on direct fetches and the OpenAlex/arXiv APIs; some relevant industry reports may have been missed.
